slides.title: Trigonometry as a Graphics Contract
slides.notes: Begin by making the appendix feel operational rather than decorative. Angles, functions, identities, inverse branches, and calculus formulas are the small contracts behind rotation code, projection code, and intersection diagnostics. Ask students to watch for two recurring questions: what is the represented geometry, and what invariant checks the result?

slides.title: Angle Data Contract
slides.notes: Use this slide to fix orientation before formulas start. The initial ray is a reference direction, the terminal ray names the result of rotation, and the sign convention is part of the data model. Radian measure is not just a unit conversion; it binds angle to arc length by s equals r theta.

slides.title: Unit-Circle Functions
slides.notes: Connect the right-triangle mnemonic to a full circular definition. Once the terminal point is stored as x and y on the unit circle, sine and cosine become coordinates, while tangent, secant, cosecant, and cotangent become quotients with explicit domain exclusions. The check x squared plus y squared equals one should feel like a unit test.

slides.title: Graphs, Domains, Periods
slides.notes: The graphs are useful because they expose both periodic repetition and forbidden inputs. Sine and cosine are bounded coordinate projections, while tangent is a quotient and therefore develops vertical asymptotes. In graphics terms, a phase shift changes where sampling begins, but it should not change the geometric circle or the invariant amplitude.

slides.title: Exponential Form
slides.notes: Present Euler form as a compression of two coordinate functions into one rotation-valued expression. The formula is not an abstraction for its own sake: multiplying complex unit numbers composes rotations, and separating real and imaginary parts recovers cosine and sine. This gives students another way to recognize addition formulas.

slides.title: Identities as Invariants
slides.notes: Treat the identities as tools for debugging, not a list to memorize. The Pythagorean identity checks whether a circular coordinate pair has drifted off the unit circle. The addition formulas check whether two rotations were composed in the intended order. The notebook habit is to turn each identity into a residual that can be asserted.

slides.title: Triangle Laws
slides.notes: Use the triangle laws as the bridge from reference trigonometry to geometric algorithms. A mesh routine, collision query, or camera calibration step often knows lengths or dot products before it knows the angle. The law of cosines turns those measurements into an angle, but numerical code must still clamp near-domain endpoints before applying arccos.

slides.title: Inverse Branches
slides.notes: This is the most practical inverse-trigonometry slide in the lecture. Principal values are useful because they make inverse functions single-valued, but a graphics computation often needs the original quadrant. Stress the difference between arctan of a ratio and atan2 of an ordered pair; the second preserves the signs that encode orientation.

slides.title: Calculus Of Circular Motion
slides.notes: Use the calculus formulas to interpret circular motion, not merely to fill a reference table. Differentiating the position p of theta gives a tangent velocity, so the derivative pair is visible in the diagram. Integrals reverse that relationship and appear whenever angular velocity or accumulated phase must be reconstructed from samples.

slides.title: Robust Angle Recovery
slides.notes: This slide turns the appendix into a routine students can actually use. The dot product alone gives an unsigned angle through arccos, but the determinant supplies orientation. Feeding both numbers to atan2 avoids quadrant ambiguity, and the reconstruction residual R of theta applied to u minus v checks that the recovered angle matches the intended rotation.

slides.title: Failure Modes
slides.notes: Frame these failures as production bugs students can recognize. A degree-radian mismatch often gives a smooth but incorrect animation. A quotient function can explode at a legitimate axis direction. A branch cut can make a continuous sweep jump. The repair strategy is always the same: name the convention, check the invariant, and report the residual.

slides.title: Recap Exercise
slides.notes: Close by asking students to assemble the full workflow rather than recall isolated formulas. A strong answer names the unit convention, chooses atan2 because orientation matters, converts only at the display boundary, and checks the result by reconstructing the rotated vector. This recap mirrors the notebook pattern: model, draw, perturb, measure, and check.
